headline: High risk of prompt injection and cascading errors from agentic-flow’s MCP/shell/git outputs into Taipy workflows; compliance risk is low but nonzero.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: agent_a can use MCP, stdin/stdout, shell, and GitHub, so it may emit raw content that agent_b could ingest in a Taipy workflow. agent_b has no documented parsing safeguards or provenance checks. Because the pairwise bridge is plausible in default orchestration and could hijack downstream instructions, I rate this high rather than medium.
conditions: IF agent_b consumes agent_a stdout, files, or MCP messages as instructions without provenance checks, injection is possible.
IF the orchestrator connects agent_a outputs into Taipy inputs or prompts, attacker-controlled content can steer agent_b.
mitigations: Add a provenance tag to every agent_a output before Taipy ingests it.
Require a human review step for any agent_a-generated instructions.
Strip executable markup and prompt-like delimiters from shared text.
Disable direct stdout-to-input wiring between the agents.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and provenance enforcement in the orchestrator.

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_a touches code, repository metadata, learning patterns, performance metrics, and task prompts, and can egress over allowlisted network paths. agent_b documents no egress and no touched data classes, so the main leakage path is agent_a exporting sensitive context into shared workflows. The pairwise risk exists in default integrations, but the blast radius is bounded by the documented surfaces.
conditions: IF agent_a is given prompts or repository data containing secrets, those contents can be forwarded over allowlisted egress.
IF agent_b receives shared workspace files produced by agent_a, those files may expose repository metadata or task prompts.
mitigations: Restrict agent_a to a redacted workspace.
Block secrets from being written to shared files.
Review allowlisted destinations before running.
Separate per-agent directories and temp paths.
requires-engineering: add DLP scanning on agent_a outputs.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: agent_a can execute shell, install packages, modify git state, and spawn subprocesses; agent_b is a data-engineering tool with no documented write or concurrency controls. The pair can conflict if both operate on the same repository or mutable workspace, especially around git state. Uncertainty about agent_b’s write surface escalates this to medium rather than low.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same git checkout, commits or working-tree changes can race.
IF agent_b mutates shared files through its workflows, agent_a shell actions can overwrite them.
mitigations: Run each agent in a separate checkout.
Serialize git writes with a lock file.
Disable package installation in shared workspaces.
Use read-only mounts for agent_b inputs.
requires-engineering: add workspace-level concurrency control.

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_a can generate analysis, build, and transfer outputs, while agent_b is a data-engineering system that may consume those outputs in pipelines. There is no documented verification layer showing that agent_b critically checks agent_a’s results before acting. That makes a default cascade plausible, but not clearly irreversible, so medium fits.
conditions: IF agent_b treats agent_a-produced files or metrics as authoritative, errors can propagate downstream.
IF agent_a emits malformed build or transfer artifacts, agent_b may ingest them without validation.
mitigations: Insert schema validation between agents.
Require checksum or signature checks on transferred artifacts.
Compare agent_a outputs against a second source.
Log and review failed validations before reruns.
requires-engineering: add automated verification gates.

E_compliance.rationale: agent_a handles Ed25519 signatures and repository metadata, while agent_b documents no sensitive data classes, residency, or retention obligations. I cannot prove a compliance breach pathway from the profiles alone, so this stays low. I do not cite agent_b data classes because the field is empty and informative; the absence of documented obligations is the relevant point.
conditions: IF regulated data is introduced into agent_a’s workflow, retention and handling policies must be checked.
IF agent_b is later configured to store or export shared artifacts, residency and retention rules may diverge.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the pair.
Document retention for shared artifacts.
Review whether signatures or metadata are sensitive.
Limit logs to minimal operational fields.
requires-engineering: map data flows to compliance controls.
